Baby & Child

Helping children explore, test and develop creative ideas

Updated: November 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A child’s idea might become a drawing, a rhythm, a different ending to a story or a new way to hold a model together. You can make room for that process without deciding whether your child is a talented artist. The useful work is in noticing a possibility, trying something and deciding what to change. These suggestions offer opportunities to explore; they are not a programme for raising intelligence or securing future success.

Make the process visible

Sometimes an activity teaches a particular technique; sometimes the child decides what to make. Both can have a place. For creative exploration, leave some decisions open instead of presenting a finished example that must be copied. A picture does not have to resemble an adult’s idea of good art to be worth discussing.

Ask about a decision you can see: which part the child chose first, or what they changed along the way. Avoid treating creative and uncreative as permanent categories of children. Being comfortable with numbers does not rule out making music, and liking drawing does not define every interest. Explore the particular activity rather than assigning an identity.

Welcome possibilities while keeping clear limits

An unusual suggestion deserves a hearing, even when it will not work as proposed. You can ask what the child wants it to do before offering a solution. For example, a bridge that keeps falling might prompt a question about which part needs support. This is a suggested conversation, not a test with a required answer.

Welcoming an idea does not mean allowing harm or promising that every plan is practical. State the limit, then look for another way to pursue the intention: a drawing of an invention can replace trying it with unsafe equipment. Keep criticism about the problem rather than the child. An unsuccessful attempt can be information about a design, not evidence of personal failure.

Let children choose a direction and learn useful techniques

Offer a manageable choice connected to an interest: making something that moves, inventing a creature or exploring a sound. A child can change direction or return to an earlier project. Do not require every interest to become a class, a competition or a long-term commitment. You can also ask whether they want company, a demonstration or room to work.

Learning a technique can make an idea easier to express. Show how to join two pieces or make a particular mark when help is wanted, then give the decision back. Repeated practice and free experimentation need not compete. There is no prescribed number of practice hours that turns a child into a creative person, and enjoyment need not lead to professional-level skill.

Create a modest collection of useful materials

Start with what is available: clean cardboard, paper, suitable drawing materials and child-appropriate tape can offer several possibilities. One box can hold a small making collection between sessions; a dedicated studio is unnecessary. Building pieces can be used for an invented design as well as a model from instructions, provided they suit the child’s age and abilities.

The point is flexibility, not deprivation. Fewer possessions do not automatically produce better ideas. A child may need a larger grip, an accessible work surface or another way to communicate a plan. Treat these supports as part of making the activity possible. Ask which material would help with the next step before buying an expensive kit advertised as a creativity booster.

Work alongside the child without taking ownership

Join an invitation or work on your own small project nearby. You might demonstrate how you compare two possible arrangements, explain why you changed your mind or admit that something did not turn out as expected. This makes your thinking available without requiring the child to copy your hobby or produce a matching object.

When a problem appears, allow a little room for the child to try, but respond when help is requested. Ask which part is difficult and offer just enough assistance for the next attempt. It is also reasonable to pause a frustrating task. Quiet exploration can be valuable; an adult does not need to narrate or question every action.

Use sound, movement and stories as other starting points

Creative work need not leave a physical object behind. An interested child could invent another verse, change a short rhythm or choose a movement to represent a character. Make space for seated movements or another comfortable way to participate. Keep sound comfortable and the movement area clear. These are invitations to make choices, not a demand to perform for others.

Research on creative dance is promising but specific. In one controlled eight-week study of 57 preschoolers, the programme group improved more on a motor-creativity test; there was no significant between-group difference in motor competence. That result does not establish that a dance session improves every kind of creativity or produces lasting gains for every child.

Separate media possibilities from promises

A screen can be a tool for making as well as watching. Depending on the child and application, possible projects include drawing a character, recording a sound sequence or arranging pictures into a story. Check what the child can actually choose and create. These examples are practical suggestions, not evidence that any particular app improves creativity.

Look at content, the child’s experience and what media use leaves less time for, including sleep, movement and relationships. Agree on boundaries together where appropriate. Watching is not automatically mindless, and a device is not automatically harmful or beneficial. Leave opportunities to carry an idea into another medium rather than making screen time the only route to exploration.

Do not turn a film finding into a creativity prescription

A 2010 study reported two experiments in which children who watched fantastical content performed better on several subsequent creativity tasks than comparison groups. The researchers did not find a change in the children’s beliefs about magic. The finding concerns responses on particular tasks; it does not establish that a named film or a short daily viewing routine creates lasting creativity.

Choose stories or programmes for their suitability and your child’s interest, not a promised mental upgrade. A playful alternative is to invent a different ending or ask what would happen if a character could solve the problem another way. There is no need to teach that fictional events are real or insist on a story that frightens the child.

Give useful feedback without making every creation a contest

Offer a concrete observation or a question about the child’s intention. For example, you might notice that a second version stands differently and ask what changed. Let the child explain what they like or still want to try. An adult’s rating, a prize or a display-worthy finish does not have to be the purpose of the activity.

This is not a rule against affection, praise or every reward. Specific positive feedback and rewards can serve useful purposes when teaching everyday behaviour. That is a different question from whether a child wants to keep exploring an idea. Keep creative invitations from becoming constant competitions, while continuing any appropriate support plan agreed with the child’s professionals.

Find inspiration without filling the calendar

A suitable performance can offer new sounds, characters or ways of moving. Check its length and intended age range, explain what to expect and allow an early exit. Afterwards, an interested child might invent a scene of their own. Attendance is optional; a costly outing is not a requirement for being a supportive parent.

Everyday observations can also supply a starting point. For example, noticing how a leaf bends might lead to a paper shape, a movement or a story. Ask what caught the child’s attention rather than assigning an elaborate project after every outing. Leave unhurried time for an idea to develop, and accept that sometimes an enjoyable experience remains just that.

Keep creative freedom within safe boundaries

Use labelled materials intended for children and follow their instructions. Non-toxic does not mean edible or suitable for every use. Avoid solvents and hazardous adult art supplies, supervise tools, store materials safely and wash hands afterwards. Check recycled items for sharp edges and unsuitable contents; do not offer old electronics for casual dismantling.

Keep choking-size pieces away from young children, and exclude loose powerful magnets, button batteries and long cords from a casual making box. Water activities require close supervision, with young children within arm’s reach. Seek immediate medical help if a child may have swallowed a magnet or button battery; do not wait for symptoms. An interesting material is never a reason to overlook its hazards.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Practitioner guidance supports choices and exploration with appropriate adult help.

The cited dance and film studies concern particular samples and measured tasks, not guaranteed lifelong creativity.

Match materials to age and access needs, and follow current safety instructions.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organise activity ideas and questions for educators. It cannot measure a child’s creative potential, certify materials or promise a developmental outcome.

When to seek help

Supervise materials and tools, avoid hazardous adult supplies and dangerous small objects, and stay close around water. Suspected swallowing of a magnet or button battery needs immediate medical help without waiting for symptoms.

Evidence notes updated: November 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Give children room to make choices, try ideas and revise them.
  • Offer techniques and help without taking over the project.
  • Use accessible materials and explore sound, movement or stories too.
  • Treat media and research findings with realistic expectations.
  • Keep feedback specific and materials safe, without making creativity a competition.

Frequently asked questions

Do tablet or phone activities stop creativity?

Not necessarily. A device can support making, but the content, the child’s choices and the wider routine matter. Drawing or recording are possible projects, not guaranteed creativity training. Keep room for sleep, movement, relationships and activities away from screens.

Which toys are best for creative exploration?

There is no single best toy. Suitable construction pieces, drawing materials and simple household materials can allow more than one outcome. Choose for safety, access and interest. A kit with instructions can teach a technique without needing to determine every later project.

Which television programme will make my child more creative?

No programme can promise that. Experiments with fantastical content found differences on subsequent tasks, not proof of lasting everyday gains. Choose age-appropriate content your child enjoys, and offer other ways to develop an idea if they are interested.

Is watching television harmful to creativity?

A blanket answer misses the context. Notice the programme, the child’s response and whether viewing crowds out other valued activities. Make space for creating and exploring without claiming that every minute of watching damages imagination.

Should I avoid all praise and rewards?

No. You can be warm and specific about what you notice. Rewards may help teach particular behaviours; they do not have to be attached to every creative activity. Ask about decisions and experiments rather than making the finished result a constant competition.

What if my child says they are not creative?

Ask about one activity they might like to try, without arguing over the label. Offer a choice, useful help and permission to stop or change direction. A reluctance to draw does not describe every interest or establish a fixed limit on what the child can explore.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
